title: The intellect the root and condition sine qua non of the will's freedom
source_text: IX. Porro quamvis Theologi Scholastici communiter statuant intellectum non esse liberum per se & formaliter, agnoscunt tamen in eo esse radicem & causam, saltem sine qua non, libertatis illius quae est in voluntate: quae, scilicet, ex eo nascitur quod intellectus humanus non tantum varia objecta voluntati proponat, sed ea quoque inter se comparet; ac in uno & eodem objecto varias boni & mali rationes percipiat, & voluntati quodammodo demonstret. Unde fit ut voluntas possit unum & idem objectum respuere, vel amplecti, & inter objecta varia istud, vel illud eligere: qua in re positum est libertatis exercitium.
pass_a_gloss: Further, although the Scholastic Theologians commonly lay down that the intellect is not free of itself and formally, yet they acknowledge that in it is the root and cause, at least sine qua non, of that liberty which is in the will: which, namely, is born from this, that the human intellect not only proposes various objects to the will, but also compares them with one another; and perceives in one and the same object various aspects of good and evil, and in some way shows them to the will. Whence it comes that the will can reject or embrace one and the same object, and among various objects choose this or that: in which thing the exercise of liberty is placed.
pass_b_english: The scholastic theologians generally say the intellect is not free in itself and formally. Still they grant that it holds the root and cause of the will's freedom, at the least as the condition without which there would be none.

That freedom arises because the human intellect does more than set different objects before the will. It also weighs them against each other, sees different aspects of good and evil in a single object, and in a manner points them out to the will.
That is why the will can refuse or accept the same object and choose this or that among many, and in this the use of freedom consists.

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
